_comment: Golden eval set for the portfolio RAG chat. Each entry: a question; its category and depth; an expectation that drives scoring; expected_sources (content-dir-relative paths that MUST be retrieved, for must_retrieve questions); and expected_points (the answer facts, each literally supported by a cited source — a grading aid for the live acceptance harness, not scored by the retrieval runner). Expectations: must_retrieve (hit-rate + MRR over expected_sources); must_refuse_offcorpus (the weak-retrieval gate must refuse); must_refuse_generative / must_refuse_translation (the deterministic guardrail gate must fire); must_refuse_injection (prompt + live-LLM containment — scored by evals/acceptance.py, NOT by run_eval). Built and adversarially verified in Phase 0: every expected_source was confirmed to exist and every expected_point checked literally against its source.

queries.question: Where does AudiobookMaker store downloaded Piper voice models, how large are they, and does Piper need a GPU or an internet connection to synthesize?
expected_points: Piper voices are cached under ~/.audiobookmaker/piper_voices (Path.home() / '.audiobookmaker' / 'piper_voices'), created on demand
Models are ~60 MB per voice, downloaded on first use; nothing is bundled with the installer
Piper runs offline on CPU: requires_gpu = False and requires_internet = False (internet only needed when downloading a new voice)

queries.question: Why does AudiobookMaker merge very short text chunks before handing them to Chatterbox, and how does that merge actually work?
expected_points: Neural TTS models (Chatterbox specifically) behave pathologically on tiny inputs: a 7-character fragment like 'vuoksi,' makes the model ramble for 10+ seconds, and that garbage audio passes VAD-based silence detection straight into the assembled book
_merge_short_chunks folds any chunk shorter than min_chars into the preceding chunk, allowing a modest overflow past max_chars (a 230-char chunk reads fine; a 7-char one does not)
The behavior is opt-in: the Chatterbox runner sets min_chars, while the online engines (which chunk at 3000 chars and never see fragments that small) leave it at the default 0 and are unaffected

queries.question: Why does AudiobookMaker run Chatterbox in a separate Python venv and subprocess, and why does the bridge strip certain environment variables before launching it?
expected_points: Chatterbox's PyTorch + CUDA dependencies (~15 GB of model weights) live in an isolated Python 3.11 venv to keep the main app bundle below ~200 MB and avoid dependency conflicts

The frozen PyInstaller app sets PYTHONPATH to its bundled packages; when the Chatterbox subprocess inherited that PYTHONPATH the venv interpreter preferred the app's packages and model load failed with 'Could not import module LlamaModel' even though the venv was healthy

isolated_python_env() strips PYTHONPATH, PYTHONHOME, and PYTHONSTARTUP and sets PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1, and the same environment is used for both the synthesis run and the post-install smoke test so the verified and synthesis environments cannot diverge

queries.question: What is claude-continue's tech stack, and what does it depend on at runtime?
expected_points: Python 3.9+ using only the standard library — zero runtime third-party Python packages
Tkinter is used for the GUI
PyInstaller is used at build time only (not a runtime dependency)
At runtime it also relies on Node via `npx ccusage`

queries.question: Why does claude-continue verify-and-retry after firing instead of trusting the ccusage reset estimate?
expected_points: ccusage floors each window's startTime to the whole hour, so its reset estimate can fire up to an hour early (e.g. a 09:23 first message yields a 14:00 endTime but a real 14:23 reset)
After firing, `_verify_and_retry()` re-reads ccusage and checks whether a new active block appeared whose reset_at is later than the one just fired against
If the block has not advanced, it re-fires `continue` every retry_interval (default 120 s) up to retry_cap (default 30) attempts, for roughly one hour of retry coverage

The doc calls this bounded verify-and-retry the correctness mechanism — it turns an occasionally-wrong (approximate) estimate into a correctness-preserving design because the retry window covers the plausible early-estimate range; a separate `reset_offset` correction is added to the estimate before the buffer to compensate for the floored start time

queries.question: Why did the Windows build switch from a single-file PyInstaller exe to a one-dir build?
expected_points: The single-file exe unpacked python311.dll and the rest of the runtime into %TEMP% on every launch, which heuristic antivirus (specifically IPVanish Threat Protection) flagged as malware behavior and blocked
Version 0.9.0 switched to a one-dir build where the runtime DLLs live permanently in an `_internal\` folder beside the exe, scanned once on install and never re-extracted

UPX compression was explicitly disabled (it inflates false-positive rates on Windows and corrupts macOS binaries) and version metadata (CompanyName, ProductName, file version) was added to the exe resource block
The change forced a redesign of the self-update to swap entire directories rather than single files

queries.question: What rate-limit thresholds and time window does HRM enforce, and what database mechanism makes the check atomic against concurrent requests?
expected_points: 30 requests per window for actions (MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW = 30) and 10 per window for auth endpoints (AUTH_MAX_REQUESTS = 10)
A 1-minute / 60-second window (RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS = 60 * 1000)
Atomicity comes from a single raw SQL `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (identifier, action) DO UPDATE ... RETURNING count` so two concurrent requests cannot both read the same pre-increment count
Authenticated requests are keyed by `user:<id>` while anonymous requests are keyed by `ip:<ip>` (rateLimitAuth always keys on IP)

queries.question: Why does HRM promote the first OAuth user to superuser inside a SERIALIZABLE transaction instead of a plain read-count-then-create?
expected_points: The naive read-user-count-then-create is a TOCTOU race: two simultaneous first-time sign-ins both read count === 0 and both receive superuser
SERIALIZABLE isolation makes PostgreSQL detect the phantom-read condition and abort one of the concurrent transactions with a serialization failure
upsert handles the same email arriving in two concurrent sign-ins without a unique-constraint violation
The logic runs in the NextAuth signIn callback

queries.question: How does HRM keep JWT-embedded permissions fresh without a database round-trip on every request, and what is the tradeoff that enables force-logout?
expected_points: A permissionsVersion integer on the User table lets the JWT callback fetch only id/role/permissionsVersion on the common path; the full permissions join is skipped when the token's version matches the DB
The full permissions relation is fetched only on sign-in or when versions (or role) diverge
Pure JWTs cannot be revoked, so a UserSession table provides force-logout: the callback checks the token's embedded sessionId still has active:true and returns an empty token if it was deactivated

lastActiveAt updates are throttled to at most once per 60 seconds and wrapped in a silent .catch (flagged as ERR-04) — the accepted tradeoff is that a DB-down condition lets stale sessions keep passing validity checks

queries.question: How does Platform fetch World of Warcraft character data, and what validation, caching, and timeout settings does the Raider.IO integration use?
expected_points: Character data is fetched from the Raider.IO endpoint https://raider.io/api/v1/characters/profile
The response is validated with a Zod schema (RaiderIoResponseSchema); a parse failure throws ActionError("raiderIoError")
The fetch is cached with a 24-hour Next.js revalidate window and the tag "raiderio" (next: { revalidate: 60 * 60 * 24, tags: ["raiderio"] })
A 10-second abort timeout is set via AbortSignal.timeout(10000); HTTP 400/404 surface as characterNotFound and other non-OK statuses as raiderIoError

queries.question: Why does Platform embed the resolved permission set in the JWT, and how do an admin's permission or role changes reach active sessions without forcing a sign-out?
expected_points: The resolved permission map is embedded in the JWT at sign-in to avoid a per-request database read for the common case
A permissionsVersion integer column on User is incremented on every permission/role change and lets the JWT callback detect stale tokens

The jwt callback skips the DB check when the token was synced within a 5-minute TTL (lastDbSync); otherwise it runs a lightweight findUnique (id/alias/role/permissionsVersion) and rebuilds permissions only on a version (or role) mismatch

The tradeoff is a worst-case propagation delay of 5 minutes; the motivation is recorded in the commit perf(web): cut serverless CPU usage, since the original code ran findUnique on every token refresh / page navigation

queries.question: Why does Platform run both tenants and the demo experience on a single shared PostgreSQL database instead of separate databases, and what isolation and leak risks does that create?
expected_points: Every content row carries a tenant column plus an optional sessionId discriminator, and all queries filter through getTenantFilter(); demo sessions set sessionId to the DemoSession id while real users have sessionId = null
A single database keeps deployment simple (one connection pool) and lets a superuser switch tenants at runtime via a TopBar toggle

seedDemoData runs in a single prisma.$transaction and namespaces slugs/emails with a sessionId prefix (${seed.slug}-${sessionId.slice(0,8)}) to avoid unique-constraint collisions when multiple demo sessions are alive

Identified leak risks: the tenant cookie was set httpOnly:false (client JS could read/exfiltrate it) and was fixed to httpOnly:true, and CustomQuest originally lacked a sessionId so demo quests were visible to real users until a column was added

queries.question: What technologies and versions does the portfolio site's stack use, and what is the minimum Node runtime?
expected_points: Astro 6 (island architecture — zero framework runtime on pages with no interactive islands)
Three.js 0.184 and GSAP + ScrollTrigger 3.15, both dynamically imported per-page
Tailwind CSS v4 (4.2) and TypeScript 6 in strict mode with noUncheckedIndexedAccess
Node 22 is the runtime floor (ADR 0007), adopted in the Astro 5 to Astro 6 upgrade

queries.question: Why doesn't the site just use HTML5 audio loop for its music bed, and how does the dual-deck crossfade work instead?
expected_points: HTML5 loop re-buffers the start of the file before resuming, producing a 50–200 ms silent gap at the join that is consistently audible in Safari
Two <audio> decks share the same source; an equal-power crossfade (fadeOut = cos((PI/2)*t), fadeIn = sin((PI/2)*t)) over the last 1.5 s keeps combined power constant because cos^2 + sin^2 = 1
Web Audio API AudioBufferSourceNode was rejected because it requires decoding the whole track into a float32 buffer in memory and complicates the autoplay-unlock flow for marginal gain
A linear crossfade was rejected because both decks at 50% is quieter than one at 100%, causing a perceived loudness dip at the midpoint

queries.question: How does the portfolio handle Three.js scene lifecycle to avoid GPU memory leaks, and why were the dispose helpers and the DPR cap extracted?
expected_points: Because it is a static MPA with hard navigations and no client-side router, each scene initializes once and must dispose every allocation on beforeunload — missing one item leaks GPU memory each time a visitor navigates back in the same tab
disposeMaterial was extracted because Three.js types Object3D.material as Material | Material[], so every call site otherwise repeats the array check

disposePasses iterates composer.passes calling pass.dispose() before composer.dispose(), because composer.dispose() does not release the ShaderMaterial / fullscreen-quad geometry owned by RenderPass and OutputPass

The DPR is capped at 1.5 (not the native up-to-3) in resolvePixelRatio, shared by both createRenderer and createResizeHandler so a past regression that re-upgraded DPR to 2 on resize cannot recur; uncapped, the home scene burned ~40–60% of one CPU core on high-refresh displays

queries.question: Which external book-search APIs does ReadLog call, how many results does each request, and what happens when the Google Books API key isn't set?
expected_points: Open Library search (openlibrary.ts) hits openlibrary.org/search.json with limit=15 and needs no API key
Google Books search (googlebooks.ts) hits www.googleapis.com/books/v1/volumes with maxResults=15 using GOOGLE_BOOKS_API_KEY
If GOOGLE_BOOKS_API_KEY is absent (or the query is blank), searchGoogleBooks returns an empty array
Google Books synthesizes a subtitle like `Book <bookDisplayNumber>` from volumeInfo.seriesInfo.bookDisplayNumber

queries.question: After caching was added, ReadLog's library and home-feed pages started throwing `toISOString is not a function` — why did that happen and how was it fixed?
expected_points: unstable_cache serializes its return value to JSON and deserializes it on cache hits, so Prisma Date objects come back as strings
On a cache miss Prisma returned a real Date and `.toISOString()` worked; on a cache hit the value was a string, throwing `TypeError: entry.finishedAt.toISOString is not a function`
The fix wrapped every date read in `new Date(...)` before calling `.toISOString()`
It was applied to both src/app/library/page.tsx and src/app/page.tsx, since cached actions must treat dates as string | Date regardless of the inferred Prisma type

queries.question: Why does ReadLog use the Neon serverless adapter instead of a standard Prisma client, and what problem does the db.ts singleton solve?
expected_points: A standard Prisma client uses TCP connections, which are incompatible with Vercel's function model (functions cold-boot, handle a request, shut down — leaving TCP connections dangling or crashing the pool)
@prisma/adapter-neon over @neondatabase/serverless routes DB traffic over HTTP/WebSocket instead of raw TCP

The db.ts singleton (`globalForPrisma.prisma ?? createPrismaClient()`) avoids instantiating a new client on every dev hot-reload, while a fresh client is created per production cold start because globalForPrisma.prisma is only assigned when NODE_ENV !== 'production'

queries.question: How does ReadLog's EF Core model store the reading-format enum, and what database-level constraints does it put on ratings and on duplicate entries?
expected_points: Format is stored via HasConversion<string>() (HasMaxLength 16) so the column holds the readable name 'Book'/'Audiobook'/'Ebook' rather than an ordinal
A check constraint CK_ReadEntry_Rating enforces [Rating] IS NULL OR ([Rating] >= 0 AND [Rating] <= 5)
A composite unique index on (UserId, BookId, FinishedAt) prevents duplicate reads of the same book on the same finished date
Book.OpenLibraryId has a unique index

queries.question: Two users logging the same book at the same time could collide on the unique OpenLibraryId index. How does GetOrCreateBookAsync handle that race, and what failure is it careful NOT to swallow?
expected_points: Concurrent inserts of the same OpenLibraryId would violate the unique index, raising a DbUpdateException
On that exception it detaches the failed entity and re-queries for the existing row with the same OpenLibraryId, returning the winner if found (and logging the lost race)
If no winning row exists, the original exception is re-thrown, so a non-race failure such as a locked database is not silently mislabeled as a tolerated race

queries.question: Why does ReadLog's Google external-login callback refuse to automatically link a Google sign-in to an existing local account that shares the same email address?
expected_points: If a Google login arrives for an email that already has a local password account, the callback refuses to auto-link and asks the user to sign in locally first
An email-string match alone is not proof of ownership
Silently attaching the Google provider to a pre-existing password account would let an attacker who pre-created an account with the victim's email hijack it the moment the victim uses Google sign-in

queries.question: How does AudioBus track mute state, what categories does it use, and how is the effective mute computed?
expected_points: AudioBus is the single source of truth for mute state across three categories: music, voice, and sfx
Effective mute for a category is computed as master || category (isMuted returns masterMuted || categoryMuted[category])
Engines self-register via audioBus.register(category, this) in their constructor, and the bus synchronously seeds the new engine with the current effective mute on register
setMasterMuted / setCategoryMuted use a snapshot-before / applyDiff-after pass so setMuted only fans out to categories whose effective mute actually changed (avoiding redundant calls)

queries.question: Why does SceneRig.dispose() call renderer.forceContextLoss() before dispose(), and why must the galaxy canvas be keyed on currentSolarSystemId?
expected_points: Without forceContextLoss() the WebGL context lingers until garbage collection during rapid galaxy-to-combat cycling and can exhaust the browser's per-page WebGL context budget (browsers cap concurrent contexts at roughly 8-16 — this figure appears only in deepdive.md)
forceContextLoss() makes the canvas's context permanently unrecoverable, which is only safe when the canvas DOM element is also going away (galaxy→combat unmount or page nav)

On a warp between solar systems the same GameCanvas stays mounted and would reuse the same canvas, so GameCanvas.tsx keys the galaxy <canvas> on currentSolarSystemId to force React to mount a fresh DOM element each warp

Both files carry mirrored INVARIANT comments: dropping the key prop without removing the forceContextLoss() call breaks warp deterministically (the next new THREE.WebGLRenderer({canvas}) would throw on the permanently-lost context)

queries.question: What caused the May 2026 save wipe and how was it fixed?
expected_points: Root cause (2026-05-02): three anti-cheat guards checked that fields did not grow too fast, but none checked for shrinkage, so a buggy client posting credits=0 and completedMissions=[] passed the growth guards and overwrote a real player's progression with empty state
The fix shipped validateNoRegression, which rejects any POST where completedMissions, unlockedPlanets, or playedTimeSeconds is smaller than the stored server row, returning HTTP 422 save_regression

422 rejections were changed from permanent (drop the snapshot) to transient (hold in localStorage and retry after the next successful loadSave), plus a client-side hydration gate that stops saveNow() posting INITIAL_STATE before loadSave hydrates
Forensic and structural follow-ups: the save_audit table (one row per POST attempt) and an append-only save_snapshots table dual-written on every successful save as the recovery surface

queries.question: What does the scripts/export.js tool do, and what dependencies does it need?
expected_points: It strips the leading metadata-header comment block from a Strudel pattern file and prints a paste-ready version to stdout, optionally copying to the clipboard with --copy
It recognizes metadata keys Genre, Tempo, Key, Role, Notes, BPM, and Description, handling both a run of consecutive // header lines and a leading /* */ block comment whose body is metadata-only
It uses no dependencies beyond Node's stdlib — only fs, path, and child_process
Clipboard copy is platform-detected (clip.exe on win32, pbcopy on darwin, xclip on linux) and degrades gracefully to stdout-only if the clipboard tool is unavailable

queries.question: Why do these Strudel tracks set tempo with values like .cpm(33) for 132 BPM instead of .cpm(132), and what bug forced that?
expected_points: Strudel's .cpm() counts cycles (bars) per minute, not beats; in the default 4/4 convention one cycle equals one bar of four beats
The first jaakko-kulta-future-bass version used .cpm(132) intending 132 BPM, but at four kicks per bar that fired 132 bars x 4 = 528 kicks per minute — gabber, not trance
The fix and now-embedded formula is BPM / 4 = cpm (for standard 4/4 with a bd*4 kick), so .cpm(33) gives 33 cycles x 4 beats = 132 BPM
The bug is subtle because the Strudel REPL does not error — the pattern just runs at the wrong speed — so the formula was saved into CLAUDE.md and documented inline in every track

queries.question: How are full-song arrangements (intro / main / break / etc.) achieved without using cat() to sequence sections, and what is the downside of that approach?
expected_points: Arrangement uses .mask() with long binary strings — one digit per bar — that gate each layer to the cycles where the mask value is truthy, so all sections live in a single stack() expression instead of being sequenced by cat()
Every layer carries its own mask string, so e.g. drums drop out in the break while hats keep playing — the same section expressed as different binary digits per voice

The advantage over cat() (which forces a procedural introduce-then-main-then-break sequence) is that every musical voice stays visible simultaneously in a flat layout, so the agent can read and edit any layer without mentally simulating the section order
The tradeoff is that mask strings are opaque: a 32-digit binary string requires counting positions to audit

queries.question: Which of Mikko's projects use PostgreSQL, and is there one that deliberately chose a different database?
expected_points: HRM, Platform, Spacepotatis, and ReadLog all use PostgreSQL
HRM additionally runs MongoDB alongside Postgres for an immutable, hash-chained audit log (a dual-database design)
Spacepotatis's PostgreSQL is hosted on Neon and accessed through Kysely (a typed SQL query builder) rather than a full ORM
ReadLog .NET is the deliberate outlier: it uses SQLite (a local file persisted on Azure /home) specifically to avoid any paid database tier, keeping infrastructure cost at $0

queries.question: How do Mikko's projects connect to or depend on one another?
expected_points: AudiobookMaker (Chatterbox engine) generates all in-game voice and story narration for Spacepotatis
strudel-patterns scores Spacepotatis (galaxy overworld, mission themes, story narration bed) and also composes the looping music bed for the mikkonumminen.dev portfolio landing page
Platform consumes HRM as a git submodule, sharing the same authentication layer and audit log
The portfolio site is intentionally separate from the production stack used in HRM and Platform, but its music bed comes from strudel-patterns

queries.question: Which of Mikko's projects are not built on the TypeScript/JavaScript stack, and what languages do they use instead?
expected_points: AudiobookMaker is written in Python (PyMuPDF, edge-tts, Piper, Chatterbox, PyTorch, CustomTkinter, packaged with PyInstaller and Inno Setup)
claude-continue is also Python (3.9+) and notably uses the standard library only — zero runtime third-party packages beyond Node for npx ccusage
ReadLog .NET is written in C# on .NET 8 LTS with ASP.NET Core Razor Pages and EF Core, a deliberate port of the original TypeScript/Next.js ReadLog
The remaining projects (HRM, Platform, Spacepotatis, ReadLog, Portfolio, strudel-patterns) are TypeScript/JavaScript

queries.question: Which of Mikko's projects has the most unusual or heavily layered rendering / tech stack, and what makes it stand out?
expected_points: Spacepotatis layers three rendering systems in one project: Next.js 16 + React 19 wraps a Phaser 4 combat scene, while Three.js + GSAP power the galaxy view and the animated camera transition into combat
Spacepotatis was built from empty repo to live browser game in 12 days (about 475 commits, ~1300 tests)
strudel-patterns is unusual in a different way: live-coded algorithmic music written in Strudel, a JavaScript pattern engine and port of TidalCycles, using the Web Audio API
The portfolio also combines Three.js + GSAP but on a fully static Astro site, with no Phaser/game layer

queries.question: How do Mikko's projects handle user authentication, and which one is the outlier?
expected_points: Most projects authenticate via NextAuth with Google OAuth (ReadLog, Spacepotatis, HRM, Platform)
HRM and Platform additionally support GitHub OAuth, and Platform offers a zero-credential demo mode
Spacepotatis makes auth optional — you can play without signing in, or opt in for cloud saves and a leaderboard slot

ReadLog .NET is the outlier: it uses ASP.NET Core Identity with local email/password accounts plus optional Google, and adds an account-takeover guard that refuses to auto-link a Google login to a pre-existing local account by email alone

queries.question: Why does mikkonumminen.dev use Astro's static output mode instead of hybrid or server-side rendering, and what concrete constraints enforce that choice?
expected_points: Portability is a deliberate requirement: static output prevents lock-in to any one provider's proprietary runtime and avoids introducing a billing surface tied to compute.
Hybrid mode was rejected because it introduces a Node.js / edge function runtime as a deployment dependency, eliminating the 'config swap' portability guarantee.
A nonce-based CSP would require a per-request nonce plumbed through every inline tag, which is incompatible with fully static output.
Locale negotiation is performed at build time (separate HTML trees per locale) and at load time in the browser; no Accept-Language middleware runs at the CDN or server layer.

queries.question: Why is the RAG chat backend implemented as a separate service rather than as an SSR route or edge function on the Astro site itself?
expected_points: An SSR or edge function approach was rejected because it directly contradicts ADR 0002, binds the deployment to a runtime, and re-opens the server-side surfaces ADR 0002 deliberately closed.
A hosted LLM or cloud vector DB was rejected because it introduces a per-token cost and a per-request billing surface; the locked decision is that nothing costs anything per query.
The chat is progressive enhancement, never a regression: if the backend or model is unreachable, the terminal stays in its scripted-only mode with no visual difference.
Both the embedding model and the generation model are local; the database is a local container with a named volume — no hosted model, no paid API, no cloud database.

queries.question: Why does the RAG chat use layered architectural defenses instead of relying solely on a hardened system prompt to keep the model on-topic?
expected_points: The weights are fixed and public; a determined user can out-argue any wording, so prompt instructions are a real layer but cannot be the only line of defense for a publicly exposed endpoint.
The design uses controls that sit in code around the model rather than relying on prompt wording alone, so a breach of any one layer is caught by another (defense in depth).

Two deterministic pre-retrieval task gates (is_generative_request and is_translation_request) decline requests before retrieval, because these task requests often name an on-corpus topic so retrieval alone would not catch them.
LLM_NUM_PREDICT (default 512) is a hard num_predict cap, so no single answer can dump a large document regardless of what the prompt is talked into.

queries.question: Why did the RAG chat move from pure dense vector retrieval to a hybrid dense-plus-lexical approach, and what measured improvement justified the change?
expected_points: Dense embeddings miss exact identifiers: cosine similarity over bge-small-en-v1.5 is strong on paraphrase but weak on the literal token, so a query naming an exact string does not reliably pull the chunk containing it.
The original corpus was README-level prose only, so deep technical questions had no grounded answer because the implementing source was never indexed.

Dense pgvector cosine and lexical BM25-style full-text (websearch_to_tsquery + ts_rank) run as two ranked lists fused with reciprocal rank fusion: score = sum of weight / (RRF_K + rank) across both lists.
Retrieval hit-rate improved +0.059 (dense to hybrid) on the run_eval question set — the lexical channel recovers the exact-identifier queries dense alone missed.

queries.question: How does the chat assistant handle sensitive or personal data?
expected_points: Data is classified at ingest; anything marked personal data is never loaded into the assistant's memory (isolation at the door) rather than filtered out afterwards.

Person references are replaced with neutral stand-in tokens before the assistant reads them, and the key mapping a token back to a name is kept in a separate, access-controlled store the assistant cannot open.
Access is role-based and applied before retrieval; the role is decided by the system, not claimed by the visitor.

It runs on local infrastructure with no outbound path for sensitive data, and it is presented as a reference implementation, not a certified 'GDPR-compliant' product — the legal assessment is left to a data protection officer.
